scenes.narration: Alphabet, the company behind Google, is worth about three point five two trillion dollars. That's every share class, at the close on November tenth, twenty twenty-six. And by our math, that's about a hundred and seventy-eight times the free cash flow it generated over the last twelve months.

Here's why that number looks so strange. In those twelve months, Alphabet spent about one hundred and sixty billion dollars on property and equipment, eighty-nine percent of its operating cash. Free cash flow was negative in each of the last two quarters. And this year, instead of buying back stock, Alphabet sold new stock.
So what is this price actually betting on? What has to happen for all that spending to pay off? And what could break the story?

In the next few minutes, we open the machine, follow the cash into the data centers and the new shares, run the numbers on what's priced in, and finish with the three numbers to watch when Alphabet reports next.
Quick note. This isn't financial advice. Everything here comes from Alphabet's own filings and our own math, dated, so you can decide for yourself.

scenes.narration: In twenty twenty-five, Alphabet brought in about four hundred and three billion dollars. Google Services, meaning Search, YouTube and the subscriptions, made about three hundred and forty-three billion dollars, at an operating margin of about forty-one percent. Google Cloud made about fifty-nine billion dollars. And the Other Bets, like Waymo, lost about seven and a half billion dollars. More than seventy percent of all revenue still came from advertising.

The core is still Search. Over the last twelve months, Search and other brought in about two hundred and fifty billion dollars, by our math, about fifty-three percent of everything. In the September quarter it grew twelve percent, with paid clicks up eight percent. YouTube ads added another about forty-four billion dollars over the year.

But the fastest engine is now Cloud. In the September quarter, Google Cloud made thirty point seven billion dollars, up a hundred and three percent, at an operating margin of about thirty-six percent. Part of that growth is a new kind of sale. Alphabet now sells its own A I chip systems, called T P Us, to customers. And the Cloud backlog stands at about five hundred and sixty-eight billion dollars.

That shift shows up on the map too. In the September quarter, the United States made up fifty-three percent of revenue, growing thirty-nine percent, up from forty-eight percent of the total last year, in line with that American cloud and chip demand. And advertising fell to about sixty-four percent of quarterly revenue, from more than seventy percent last year. Impressions on partner sites dropped fourteen percent. Sundar Pichai says the company is now on a half trillion dollar revenue run rate. That's his framing, but the math roughly checks out.

Let me draw the machine. Here is Google Services, the big profitable engine. Here is Google Cloud, the fast one. Here are the Other Bets, still losing money. And this arrow is the one the market watches now, the backlog flowing into Cloud revenue.

scenes.narration: A machine that profitable throws off a lot of cash. So where did it all go?

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: Operating cash flow over the last twelve months was about one hundred and eighty billion dollars. Net income was even higher, at about two hundred and thirty-six billion dollars, but about about one hundred and thirty billion dollars of that was gains on stakes in other companies, mostly on paper. Capex took about one hundred and sixty billion dollars. What was left, the free cash flow, was about twenty billion dollars, by our math.

The last two quarters show the trend. Free cash flow was minus five point nine billion dollars in the June quarter, and minus nine point one billion dollars in September. The company says it expects to significantly increase its investment in technical infrastructure this year, compared with last year. So the bill is still rising.

To pay for it, Alphabet raised money. This year it sold about forty-three billion dollars of new common stock, plus about nineteen billion dollars of preferred stock that converts into shares later. Long-term debt went from about forty-seven billion dollars at the end of last year to about one hundred and twenty-six billion dollars. And it still has about twenty-eight billion dollars of room to sell more shares on the market.

Meanwhile, the buybacks stopped. Alphabet repurchased no stock at all in the first nine months of this year. It still paid about about eleven billion dollars in dividends over the last twelve months. But the share count rose one point eight percent in a year, after years of shrinking.

There's also a strange pile of investments on the balance sheet. Alphabet holds about seventy-five billion dollars of SpaceX shares, which it can't sell right away, and one unnamed private company carried at about one hundred and twenty-eight billion dollars. Together, by our math, that's about about six percent of Alphabet's own market value. Those are marks, not cash, and they swing. In the September quarter, mostly SpaceX, they cost about about eight billion dollars on paper. And the new shares sold in June went out at about about three hundred and fifty-five dollars each. Today's price is nineteen percent lower.

Let me draw where twelve months of operating cash went. Here is the operating cash bar. Here is the capex bar, eating almost all of it. Here is what's left, the free cash flow. And here is the new stock it sold this year, just to keep going. The cash is coming in from outside now.

scenes.narration: Which brings us to the big question. At three and a half trillion dollars, what are you paying for?

scenes.narration: Three quick lenses first, all our math on the last twelve months. Price to earnings, about fifteen times, but strip out those paper gains and it's closer to about twenty-six times. Free cash flow yield, about zero point six percent. Operating cash flow yield, about five percent. The gap between those last two is the data center bill.

So for a company in a building spree, we use a proxy. We take operating cash and subtract depreciation, about about twenty-eight billion dollars a year, as a rough stand-in for the spending needed just to keep things running. That leaves about one hundred and fifty-two billion dollars, a yield of about four point three percent. It's a proxy, and it assumes capex eventually falls back toward that level.

Now let's run it backwards. What growth in that cash, for ten years, makes today's price work, before slowing to three percent? With an eight percent discount rate, about four and a half percent a year. With ten percent, about nine percent. But run the same math on today's actual free cash flow, and the answer jumps to between about thirty-one percent and about thirty-eight percent a year.

So the real question is the capex. Here's one more lens, our rough illustration. If Alphabet keeps spending at today's pace, every dollar of capex has to add about about seventeen cents to about twenty-nine cents of extra operating cash every year, within a decade, for the price to make sense.

Let me draw the two answers. Here is the growth the price needs if capex calms down. Here it is at the higher rate. And here is what it needs if capex stays where it is. Same company, same price. The difference is the spending.

scenes.narration: Number one, the Cloud backlog turns into revenue. Alphabet expects to recognize just over fifty-five percent of its backlog over the next two years, about about three hundred and twelve billion dollars by our math. One caution. Alphabet changed how it counts the backlog this year, so the jump from last year is not like for like.

Number two, the spending starts paying back. Capex is eating eighty-nine percent of operating cash, and the company expects to keep raising it. For the price to work, free cash flow has to climb back, and then keep climbing for years.

Number three, Search holds up. It is still about about fifty-three percent of revenue, and it has to keep growing while A I changes how people search, and while a court order forces Google to share some search data with rivals.

And number four, the funding gap closes. This year took new shares and new debt. To stop the dilution, operating cash has to catch up with capex, so Alphabet can go back to shrinking its share count instead of growing it.

scenes.narration: Now the other side of the scale.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: Risk one is the build-out itself. Alphabet's own filing says its investments may not result in an adequate return. It has about eight hundred billion dollars of commitments, mostly long-term supply deals, plus guarantees and repurchase promises on some hardware. If demand falls short, it could be left with capacity it can't easily use.

Risk two is the courts. The search judgment restricts how Google distributes its services. In ad tech, the judge rejected a breakup but ordered other remedies, and Google plans to appeal. In Europe, Alphabet paid five point two billion dollars for the Android fine this summer. And it has about fourteen billion dollars set aside for fines and settlements.

And the bills from Europe keep coming. The European ad tech fine was booked as a three and a half billion dollars charge, and the two digital markets decisions added another one billion dollars last quarter, all under appeal. A Swedish price comparison site won about about two point one billion dollars in damages, also under appeal. A Texas trial on ad tech is still ahead, and for that one Alphabet says it can't estimate a possible loss.

Risk three is control and dilution. The founders' special shares carry about about fifty-three percent of the votes. And the filing now warns that new share sales could depress the stock price. Reported profits will also keep swinging with the value of its stakes in other companies.

And the upside the price might not fully include. Alphabet says the Gemini app has reached one billion users. T P U systems are becoming a product line of their own. And its stakes in SpaceX and one private company are marked at about about two hundred billion dollars. Those are marks, not cash, so we won't treat them as money in the bank.

scenes.narration: So, what should you watch?

Here's the scorecard for the next report, expected in early February twenty twenty-seven, our estimate. One, Google Cloud revenue and margin, after thirty point seven billion dollars last quarter. Two, capex and free cash flow, after minus nine point one billion dollars, and what Alphabet says about spending in twenty twenty-seven. Three, Search growth, and the share count. If those hold up, the story the price is telling keeps holding up. If they crack, the spending gets much harder to defend.
That's Alphabet, November twenty twenty-six edition. We'll update it after every report, with new numbers and the same three questions. What's priced in, what has to happen, and what could go wrong.
